summary: Extends the LDP and IGP synchronization mechanism of RFC 5443 to broadcast links with more than one LDP peer, where metric increase only applies to the link as a whole. It updates RFC 5443 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router joins a shared network, the network's other routers can start sending traffic to it before the label information has arrived, and that traffic is dropped. This memo describes a way to hold the new router back until the labels are in place, without disturbing the traffic that was already flowing.

how does ldp igp sync work on broadcast networks
subtitle: How a router can bring up a shared LAN link without black-holing traffic while LDP catches up.

tldr.problem: The LDP and IGP synchronization mechanism in RFC 5443 raises a link's cost while labels are still being exchanged, but on a broadcast link the cost can only be raised for the link as a whole, not for one peer.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of raising a cost, the router whose link is coming up simply keeps that link out of its link state advertisement until LDP is operational with all the peers on the network, unless the link is the only way to reach the network.
tldr.outcome: Traffic never moves onto the new link before the labels are there, so nothing is dropped, and no other router on the shared network has to change anything.

facts.value: 1 for every link except A-PE3, which is 10

today: RFC 6138 is an Informational document from February 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It updates RFC 5443 by describing how the same synchronization can be applied to broadcast networks that carry more than one LDP peer.

sections.title: What LDP IGP Synchronization Is For
sections.content:
In RFC 5443, when the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) is not fully operational on a link, the Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) advertises the link with maximum cost, to avoid transit traffic on the link if possible. When LDP becomes operational, that is, when all the label bindings have been exchanged, the link is advertised with its correct cost. This tries to ensure that the LDP label switched path is available all along the IGP shortest path.

The mechanism in RFC 5443 has limitations when applied to a broadcast link, and those limitations are described in the problem statement. A solution that does not drop traffic is given separately, and it introduces no protocol message changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic follows the shortest path the routing protocol computes. If labels have not been exchanged yet, a router can forward that traffic but has no label to put on it, so the traffic is dropped. The fix in RFC 5443 is to make the link look expensive until the labels are ready, so the traffic goes around instead.

sections.title: Why Broadcast Networks Break the Method
sections.content:
On broadcast networks, a router's Link State Advertisement (LSA) contains a single cost to the broadcast network rather than a separate cost for each peer on it. The document analyzes this with a sample topology in which routers A, B, C and E are attached to a common broadcast network, where all links have a cost of 1 except the link A-PE3, which has a cost of 10.

In one interpretation of applying RFC 5443 to broadcast networks, when a new router is discovered on a broadcast network, that network should avoid transit traffic until LDP becomes operational between all the routers on it. This can be achieved by having all the attached routers advertise maximum cost to that network, which should divert traffic that was being sent via the broadcast network. However, traffic might be inadvertently diverted to the link that just came up, and until LDP becomes operational that traffic is black-holed. There is also route churn in the entire network, so traffic that should be unaffected takes sub-optimal paths until the high-cost metric is reverted. In the sample topology, when B's link to the broadcast network comes up and is discovered by routers A, C and E, all four can start advertising maximum cost. A then has B as next hop to PE2 and has no LDP label switched path to PE2, so VPN traffic from PE1 to PE2 is black-holed at A, and the route churn at A also diverts traffic between PE1 and PE3 to the sub-optimal path PE1-A-PE3. This interpretation also requires the maximum-cost advertisement to be reverted by all routers once LDP peering between all the routers on the network is operational, which is non-trivial and needs coordination between all of them.

In another alternative interpretation, only the router whose link to the broadcast network comes up advertises maximum cost for that link, while the other routers continue to advertise the normal cost. In the sample topology, when B's link comes up it advertises a high cost to the broadcast network. After the IGP has converged but before the LDP peering A-B is operational, A has B as the next hop for PE2 and does not have an LDP label switched path to PE2. Because A's cost to reach B is not high, A-B-PE2 becomes the shortest path, and VPN traffic from PE1 to PE2 is dropped at A.
sections.plainLanguage: On a shared network the routing protocol keeps one cost for the whole network, so a router cannot say that one particular neighbour is expensive. Raising the cost therefore affects everyone, and the traffic that gets moved may land on the link that has just arrived and is not ready. The alternative fails too: the other routers still see the new router as the shortest way.

sections.title: The Solution: Keep the Link Out of the Advertisement
sections.content:
The problem exists because the Link State Database of the IGP does not describe a link coming up on a broadcast network with a high bi-directional cost to all the other routers on that network. A broadcast network is advertised as a pseudonode containing a list of routers to which the broadcast network is connected, and the cost of all these links from the pseudonode to each router is zero when computing the shortest path.

The solution removes the link that is coming up from the link state database unless it is absolutely necessary. Only the router whose link is coming up plays a role; the other routers on the broadcast network are not involved.

During the intra-area shortest path computation, an additional computation is made to detect an alternate path to a directly connected network that does not have any IGP adjacencies. If a router has a directly connected network that does not have an alternate path to reach it, then the interface to that network is a cut-edge in the topology for that router. When a cut-edge goes down, the network is partitioned into two disjoint sub-graphs. Whether or not an interface is a cut-edge is what is used when an IGP adjacency comes up on that interface, and the method for determining it is described in an appendix.

During the IGP procedures, when the router's first adjacency to the broadcast network is coming up and the LSA is about to be updated with a link to the pseudonode of the broadcast interface, a check is made whether that interface is a cut-edge. If it is not, the updating of the LSA with that link to the pseudonode is postponed until LDP is operational with all the LDP peers on that broadcast interface. After LDP is operational, the LSA is updated with that link to the pseudonode and the LSA is flooded. If the interface is a cut-edge, then the updating of the LSA MUST NOT be delayed by LDP's operational state. The IGP and LDP adjacency bring-up procedures are otherwise unchanged, and the conditional check must be done just before the adjacency is about to be reflected in the LSA.

With OSPF, the Router-LSA is not updated with a Link Type 2, a link to a transit network, for that subnet until LDP is operational with all neighboring routers on the subnet. With IS-IS, the Link State PDU is updated with an IS Reachability TLV, or an Extended IS Reachability TLV, to the pseudonode after LDP is operational with all neighboring routers on that subnet. This solution can be introduced in a gradual manner in a network without any backward compatibility issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The new router keeps the shared network out of its own routing advertisement until the labels for all the neighbours on it have arrived. The other routers are told nothing, so traffic that was already using the shared network stays where it was. The exception is a link that is the only way to reach that network, which must be advertised immediately.

sections.title: Scope and Applicability
sections.content:
The document is agnostic to the method that detects LDP to be operational with a neighbour, and it does not define any new method to detect that LDP is operational. At the time of publication, LDP End-of-LIB (RFC 5919) seems to be the preferred method. Issues arising out of LDP not being configured on some routers or on some interfaces are not specific to the method described here and are considered outside the scope of this solution.

The method can be easily extended to point-to-point links. However, an implementation may continue to apply the method in RFC 5443 to point-to-point links and apply the method in this document to broadcast networks. Both methods can coexist in a network.

The techniques used in the solution enable LDP IGP synchronization in many scenarios where one end of the IGP adjacency does not support any LDP IGP sync method. This is an optional benefit and is for further study, and some ways of applying the technique to achieve it are discussed in an appendix. The document concludes that it complements RFC 5443 by providing a solution for broadcast networks, can coexist with that solution in a network with a combination of point-to-point links and broadcast networks, can be introduced without backward compatibility issues, and can also be used exclusively because it applies to both kinds of link.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not care how a router learns that the labels are ready; that is another protocol's job. A network can use the old method on point-to-point links and the new one on shared networks, or the new one everywhere, and it can be introduced one router at a time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not introduce any new security considerations beyond those already described in RFC 5443.

In RFC 5443, when a link is advertised with a high metric, an alternate path with a large number of hops can result in the end-to-end path having more than 255 hops and thus result in unreachability. That fact could be exploited if control of metrics falls into the hands of an attacker. The problem can even exist in a plain IP network with a link-state IGP: if the directly connected path has a higher metric than an alternate path with a Time to Live greater than 255 hops, the standard shortest path algorithm will conclude that the shortest path is the alternate path although the neighbouring node is unreachable through it. In that case the link is advertised with its normal metric and there is unreachability in the network. The document therefore introduces no new issues beyond those in a standard IGP-based IP network, and operators need to apply policy and security to the techniques used to determine and distribute the metrics used on links in their networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new, but one old trap is worth repeating: if a link is made to look expensive, the routing protocol may pick a path with more than 255 hops, and such a path cannot be forwarded at all. Anyone who can change link metrics can cause that, so metric control needs the same care as any other control.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO APPLY RFC 5443 ON A SHARED NETWORK, AND WHAT EACH COSTS

cells: Every attached router advertises maximum cost
All the routers on the shared network raise their cost to it
Traffic is diverted, possibly onto the link that just came up and is not ready, so it is dropped; the whole network churns and unrelated traffic takes worse paths
Only the new router advertises maximum cost
Only the router whose link came up raises its cost
The other routers still see the new router as the shortest way, so the traffic is dropped there instead

viz.caption: WHAT THE NEW ROUTER DOES, STEP BY STEP

items.title: Check for an alternate path
items.text: During the shortest path computation, see whether the directly connected network can be reached another way.

items.title: Decide whether the link is a cut-edge
items.text: If there is no alternate path, the interface is a cut-edge: taking it down would split the network.

items.title: Hold the link back
items.text: If it is not a cut-edge, do not put the link to the pseudonode into the link state advertisement yet.

items.title: Advertise it when LDP is ready
items.text: Once LDP is operational with every peer on the interface, update the LSA and flood it.

items.title: Never hold back a cut-edge
items.text: If the link is the only way to that network, the LSA update must not be delayed by the state of LDP.
